name: Palacio Libertad
watch: In September 2025 a fileteadores show had to remove political works hours before opening. In February 2026 officials dropped an Indigenous art biennial show.
why_flagged: A national centre that depends on the Secretaría de Cultura. Decree 897/2024 renamed it Palacio Libertad on 10 October 2024.
records_note: The centre's site carries programme, agenda and news pages, with a director named in a news post.
highlight: A cultural centre in the former Buenos Aires Central Post Office, which opened in 1928 and reopened in 2015 as a cultural centre.

overview: National cultural centre in the former Central Post Office building (Palacio de Correos) in central Buenos Aires. It depends on the national Secretaría de Cultura (La Nación, 11 September 2025).
The post office opened in 1928 to a design by Norbert Maillart begun in 1889. Its last postal bureau closed in 2005 (Wikipedia).

Néstor Kirchner proposed converting it into a cultural centre in 2005. The centre opened in May 2015 as the Centro Cultural Kirchner (CCK), in a design led by the Bares siblings that uses clear and frosted glass and stainless steel (Wikipedia).

Renamed: the Milei government announced a name change in March 2024, chose "Palacio Libertad" in May 2024, and made it official by decree 897/24 of 10 October 2024 (Wikipedia). In mid-April 2024 Culture Secretary Leonardo Cifelli ordered a plaque naming Cristina Fernández de Kirchner covered, and by 7 May 2024 a crew was removing Kirchner-name signs (La Nación, Diego Cabot, 7 May 2024).
On site: a 1,950-seat symphonic hall with an organ of about 8,000 pipes, and exhibition halls (Wikipedia).
Visiting: Wikipedia states that everything there is currently free.
details.funding_verdict: Palacio Libertad: state: the Argentine federal government through the Secretaría de Cultura

red_flags.heading: State censorship
points: Fileteadores show, September 2025: La Nación (Daniel Gigena, 11 September 2025) reported that hours before the opening of the 14th Encuentro Anual de Fileteadores the Asociación de Fileteadores announced the show would not take place and denounced censorship. It said Palacio Libertad authorities had questioned four works, three supporting Palestine and one defending public education; the show had 160 works by 152 artists. The curator, Ayelén Fagiani, said authorities called the works offensive to "la susceptibilidad del Gobierno" (translation: the government's sensitivities). Secretaría de Cultura sources said there would be no space for political demonstrations in national cultural spaces and that taking the show down was the association's decision, not the Secretaría's or the Palacio's.

Indigenous Art Biennial show, early 2026: Laura Isola wrote in Perfil (22 March 2026) that authorities pulled the Biennial's exhibition at Palacio Libertad close to its opening, citing "un cambio de programación" (a change of programming), and asked that the word "indígena" not appear, that there be no curatorial text and that the organising network's logos be removed; a Chaco-region show on the sixth floor was also blocked. The only official position Isola reports is the programming explanation, which she disputes.

red_flags.heading: Protest by artists
points: The Asociación de Fileteadores denounced the censorship in a statement reported on 11 September 2025 and said it would move all works to another venue within 24 hours. Izquierda Diario ran it on 10 September 2025.

The Biennial was shown instead at the Pabellón de Bellas Artes of the Universidad Católica Argentina in Puerto Madero, open until 12 April 2026 (Perfil, Laleska Villanueva, 20 February 2026), so the move had happened before that date.

press.overall: All criticism found concerns censorship of exhibitions, in the general press and one partisan outlet, not in art magazines.

items.title: Daniel Gigena, report on the fileteadores dispute (11 September 2025)
points: News report giving the association's claim and the Secretaría's reply.

items.title: Laura Isola, "Censura y resistencia: la disputa por el sentido del arte" (22 March 2026)
points: Calls the removal of the Indigenous Art Biennial show "un acto de censura tan torpe como deliberado" (translation: an act of censorship as clumsy as it was deliberate) and rejects the "change of programming" explanation.
Names Palacio Libertad and the national authorities.

items.title: Marilen González, "Censura al arte en el Palacio Libertad" (10 September 2025)
points: Says the national government censored four works of the fileteado show for political content, three on the genocide of the Palestinian people (the outlet's wording) and one on public education.
Written by a teacher and SUTEBA union delegate.

details.bottom_line: The money behind Palacio Libertad is the Argentine federal government's, with no sponsors or budget published on the pages read. The weak points are two exhibitions that organisers say were cancelled or blocked on officials' instructions in September 2025 and early 2026, the first disputed by the Secretaría, and the 2024 removal of Kirchner-era signs, all under the state that runs the centre. Watch whether the Secretaría de Cultura publishes programming criteria.

name: Monash University Museum of Art
funding: University-funded. Schwartz Media is the media partner. Ian Potter Sculpture Court commissions.
watch: On 25 Mar 2025 Monash indefinitely postponed Stolon Press: Flat earth (Khaled Sabsabi) under pressure; it reopened 29 May 2025.
records_note: Parent Monash University publishes an annual report with accounts; MUMA names donors on its support pages.

overview: University museum of contemporary art on the Caulfield campus of Monash University, Melbourne, known as MUMA (Wikipedia).

Grew from a fund created in 1961 by Vice Chancellor Louis Matheson to buy work by living Australian artists. Patrick McCaughey created the Monash University Gallery in 1975. It was renamed Monash University Museum of Art in 2002 (Wikipedia).
The current building on the Caulfield campus, designed by Kerstin Thompson and completed in 2010, includes the Ian Potter Sculpture Court (Wikipedia).
The ABC describes MUMA as owned by Monash University, with a 50-year history of exhibitions (ABC, 26 March 2025).
details.funding_verdict: Monash University Museum of Art: university museum: owned by Monash University
funding: Monash University owns the museum and took the decision to postpone its 2025 exhibition (ABC, 26 March 2025).

red_flags.heading: Indefinite postponement of an exhibition by the owner, 2025
points: Monash University, which owns the museum, postponed "Stolon Press: Flat earth" indefinitely in March 2025. It was due to open on 8 May after 18 months of planning and included work by Khaled Sabsabi. The ABC understood it to be the first exhibition pulled in the gallery's 50-year history (ABC, Nicola Heath and Daniel Browning, 26 March 2025).

Reason given: a Monash spokesperson said that after consulting communities the university had "identified there is a need for the Museum to deepen its collaboration and engagement on this exhibition", and that postponing "will allow this important work to be undertaken" (ArtReview, 26 March 2025). The spokesperson did not say whether the postponement was tied to Sabsabi's withdrawn Venice appointment or whether a new date had been chosen (Hyperallergic, Maya Pontone, 26 March 2025, updated 27 March).
Stolon Press's founders Tom Melick and Simryn Gill said they did not agree to it (Hyperallergic).

Penelope Benton, executive director of the National Association for the Visual Arts (NAVA), called the decision "a devastating blow to artistic and academic freedom and the integrity of our public institutions", and Ben Eltham, president of the NTEU Monash branch, said "a university censoring its own art gallery is a really bad idea" (Visual Arts Australia, 27 March 2025).

Unverified: Josh Milani, Sabsabi's gallerist, said MUMA's curators "started receiving pressure from their superiors" after Sabsabi's Venice commission was pulled; this is Milani's claim, not a Monash statement (ABC; ArtReview).
The exhibition ran from 29 May to 12 July 2025 (Milani Gallery).

press.overall: The criticism is of Monash University's 2025 postponement of one exhibition, not of MUMA's funders or programme.

items.title: no named author, "Khaled Sabsabi exhibition cancelled following Venice Biennale sacking" (26 March 2025)
points: Reports that Monash postponed the show weeks after Sabsabi and curator Michael Dagostino were withdrawn as Australia's Venice Biennale representatives, gives Milani's claim of pressure on curators and prints Monash's written reply.

items.title: Maya Pontone, "Australian University Scraps Show Featuring Work of Lebanese-Born Artist" (26 March 2025, updated 27 March)
points: Reports the postponement of the show, due to run from 8 May to 5 July, and the objection of Stolon Press's founders; quotes Milani calling it a "direct result of Creative Australia's abandonment of him".

items.title: Penelope Benton and Ben Eltham, "Monash University's postponement of exhibition featuring Khaled Sabsabi undermines artistic and academic freedom" (27 March 2025)
points: The authors argue the decision rests on assumptions about Sabsabi rather than the work, which they call quiet and meditative, and that giving in to pressure erodes trust and academic freedom.
They cite Monash's removal of the right to student protest without consultation and urge Monash to reinstate the show.

wider_context: In February 2025 Creative Australia's board voted to drop Sabsabi and curator Michael Dagostino from the 2026 Venice Biennale, after Coalition arts spokesperson Claire Chandler raised concerns in parliament about works of his from more than 15 years earlier. Mikala Tai (head of visual arts), program manager Tahmina Maskinyar and board member Lindy Lee resigned (ABC).
ArtReview and Hyperallergic tie the Monash postponement, about a month later, to that decision; Monash did not say whether the two were linked (Hyperallergic).
details.bottom_line: MUMA is a university museum owned by Monash University. The documented issue is Monash's indefinite postponement of the Sabsabi exhibition in March 2025, a first in the gallery's 50 years, which the show's organisers, NAVA and the NTEU opposed; the exhibition ran from 29 May to 12 July 2025.

name: Ў Gallery of Contemporary Art
records_note: Closed on 29 October 2020; its domain now shows only a default web-server page, with no reports, accounts, funders or board.
affiliations_note: Its complex included the Literary House Logvinov; no network or partner institution is named.

overview: Contemporary art gallery at Kastryčnickaja 19A in Minsk, with an exhibition space, the Ў wine bar, a design shop and the Literary House Logvinov (Wikipedia). It was one of the main contemporary art institutions in Belarus for more than twelve years (CIMAM).

Opened in October 2009 (Wikipedia). CIMAM describes it as a scaled-up version of the smaller gallery Podzemka. Valentina Kiseleva was director and curator and Aliaksandr Vasilievič the co-owner and creator (Wikipedia).
Named for the Belarusian letter Ў, which sets the Belarusian alphabet apart from other East Slavic alphabets (Wikipedia).

Programme: in 2010 it launched START, a programme of solo exhibitions and public discussions for young Belarusian artists. It held more than 120 exhibitions in its own building, mostly by Belarusian artists, and 14 abroad, in such places as Vilnius, Poznań, Lublin, Moscow and Stockholm, and won "Best Foreign Gallery" at ArtVilnius in 2011 and 2016 (Wikipedia).

2020: programmes were cancelled from the end of March because of the pandemic, and the space served for over three months as a warehouse and distribution hub for medical supplies for ByCovid-19. Its last exhibition, Touchable Distance, opened in late October 2020 with 28 artists from 11 countries (MoMA post, "On Forms of Political Organizing Illuminating the Future", 10 February 2021).

Closure: in summer 2020 Vasilievič, whom CIMAM calls a businessman and philanthropist, was detained while standing surety for the presidential candidate Viktar Babaryka (CIMAM, Anna Karpenko, "Nothing is There", 30 November 2021). The MoMA post says a politically motivated criminal case was brought against one of the co-owners at the end of August 2020 and the gallery office and homes were searched. Wikipedia says the gallery was dissolved on 29 October 2020. CIMAM and the MoMA post say it closed in November 2020, and CIMAM says its art directors left Belarus for security reasons. Wikipedia reports that the owners sold their stakes in the gallery and bar but kept the Ў brands.
details.funding_verdict: Ў Gallery: co-owned by Aliaksandr Vasilievič, a businessman and philanthropist
funding: Wikipedia names Aliaksandr Vasilievič as co-owner and creator, and CIMAM describes him as a businessman and philanthropist. Visitors could buy paintings and sculptures by modern Belarusian artists, and the gallery had a wine bar and a design shop (Wikipedia).
details.bottom_line: The gallery was co-owned by Aliaksandr Vasilievič, a businessman and philanthropist, and works by Belarusian artists were on sale there (Wikipedia, CIMAM). It closed in autumn 2020: a criminal case was brought against a co-owner at the end of August (MoMA post) and its art directors left Belarus (CIMAM).

name: Espacio Cultural Patiño
funding: Financed by the Patiño foundations: the Bolivian university foundation Simón I. Patiño created in 1931 and the Geneva foundation his heirs set up in 1958.
watch: Opened in 1984. One of three Patiño centres. La Paz bought two neighbouring houses and opened new galleries in 2018. Over 35,000 visitors a year.
records_note: No records of its own; the Geneva Fundación Patiño posts activity reports 2022 to 2025 and names its board, with no accounts or donor list.
affiliations_note: The centre was created in 1984 by the Fundación Simón I. Patiño, which also lists Palacio Portales and the Espacio Simón I. Patiño in Santa Cruz.

overview: Cultural centre of the Patiño foundations in the Sopocachi neighbourhood of La Paz, on Ecuador Street (Patiño foundation website).

Opened on 14 September 1984 in the Alameda building on El Prado Avenue, created by the Simón I. Patiño Foundation. It moved permanently in 1996 to the Guayaquil building on Ecuador Street (Patiño foundation website).
Named for Simón I. Patiño (1 June 1860 to 20 April 1947), who created the Fundación Universitaria Simón I. Patiño in 1931 (Wikipedia; Patiño foundation website).

Building: it bought two houses in Sopocachi, formerly the Rodó family's and Julio Sanjinés Goitia's, and opened a new building designed by the late Juan Carlos Calderón with two large exhibition halls, a theatre and a terrace facing Illimani (Los Tiempos, 7 December 2018). The foundation says a further new building on Ecuador Avenue is under construction.

On site: exhibitions of contemporary art and photography. CEDOAL, a documentation centre on Latin American arts and literature founded in 2001. CAP, a pedagogical centre since 2008. C+C Espacio, a comic centre opened in 2003. And C-Musical, begun in 2013, which preserves Bolivian audio recordings and hosts concerts (Patiño foundation website).
Visiting: no reporting found of opening days, admission or accessibility on the pages opened.
details.funding_verdict: Espacio Cultural Patiño: funded by the Patiño family foundations; the pages opened do not say where their money comes from today
funding: The Fundación Universitaria Simón I. Patiño was created in Bolivia in 1931 by Simón I. Patiño. In 1958 his heirs created the Fundación Simón I. Patiño in Geneva "to guarantee the economic sustainability" of the foundations' activities (translation); its mission is to manage the funds, and the foundations say they finance the centres they created in Bolivia (Patiño foundation website, Spanish page).

press.overall: The one press piece found, a Los Tiempos column by Lupe Cajías ("Espacio Patiño renovado", 7 December 2018), calls the building "magnífico" and the curation "impecable" (translation) and does not explain how the foundation is funded.

wider_context: Historical, not current funding: Patiño acquired a mountain near Llallagua in 1894 in settlement of a debt, found a tin vein there in 1900 and bought the Catavi, Siglo XX, Uncia and Huanuni mines; by the 1940s he controlled the international tin market. The 1952 Bolivian revolution confiscated the Patiño Mines (Wikipedia, Simón I. Patiño).

Catavi mine: Patiño acquired it in the 1900s. The largely indigenous workforce was kept in rigidly segregated conditions, away from the American managerial staff, with housing, water access, shops and toilets divided along those lines (Wikipedia, Catavi mine).

Catavi massacre, 21 December 1942: 7,000 miners on a five-day strike sought a 100% wage rise, and the military fired for six hours. The official report counted 19 dead and 400 wounded; workers' estimates reached up to 400 dead. Families lived in company huts without running water or toilets. That page does not name the mine owner; the Catavi mine page names Patiño as the owner (Wikipedia, Catavi massacre).
The Patiño biography on Wikipedia does not discuss labour conditions.
The centre belongs to foundations created by Patiño (1931) and his heirs (1958).
details.bottom_line: The centre is paid for by two family foundations; no corporate or state funder was found, and no page opened gives their income, donors or accounts. The weak point is that the origin of the funds is not stated, while the family's tin fortune has a documented history at Catavi (conditions, the 1942 massacre) that is kept here as background. Worth watching are the new building under construction and whether the Geneva foundation publishes financial detail.

name: Sesc São Paulo
funding: 2023 revenue R$3.44bn: R$2.70bn (78%) from the compulsory levy on commerce, services and tourism firms, R$209M from services, R$495M financial income.
records_note: Posts annual management reports for 2020 to 2024 with an independent audit report.
finances_note: FY2024 income BRL 3.78bn: about 79 percent compulsory levy on businesses, 14 percent financial income, 6 percent services; no grant line from a named public body (budget execution summary 2024).
affiliations_note: A regional administration of Sesc Brasil, whose Departamento Nacional is the national executive body, in the same commerce system as Senac.

overview: Network of cultural, sports and social centres in São Paulo state, run by the regional administration of the Serviço Social do Comércio (Sesc), a private non-profit institution (Wikipedia). The regional administration for the state is named on sescsp.org.br.

Sesc was created on 13 September 1946 by Decree-Law 9,853, signed by President Eurico Gaspar Dutra, and belongs to the "Sistema S" group of business-created bodies with Senac, Senai and Sesi (Wikipedia, Portuguese and English).

Its centres offer culture, education, health, leisure and sport. It is aimed at workers in commerce, services and tourism and their families but open to the public (Wikipedia, sescsp.org.br). Its Credencial Plena is a free benefit for workers in those sectors (sescsp.org.br).

Best-known centre: Sesc Pompeia, at Rua Clélia 93, converted from a 1938 oil-drum factory by Lina Bo Bardi between 1977 and 1986. It opened on 22 January 1982 with two concrete towers of sports halls joined by walkways, a theatre, library, pool, exhibition rooms and workshops (Wikipedia).
Sesc 24 de Maio, Rua 24 de Maio 109, showed "HIP-HOP 80'sp" with free admission, extended to 29 March 2026 (e-flux). Luiz Galina is named as Director of Sesc São Paulo (e-flux).
Visiting: hours and prices vary by centre.
details.funding_verdict: Sesc São Paulo: mainly a levy on companies in commerce, services and tourism
funding: Sesc's revenue comes from a tax on companies, at rates between 0.2% and 2.5% (Wikipedia, English). It is a non-profit private institution kept by businessmen in trade, services and tourism (Wikipedia).

items.title: "A censura à Judith Butler no Brasil e a reação dos artistas" (2017)
points: Not criticism of Sesc: it criticises the campaign against Butler's seminar and backs the artists' counter-campaign.
Names Sesc Pompeia as the target of the campaign. A news outlet, not art press, and partisan.

wider_context: Judith Butler seminar, 2017: Sesc Pompeia hosted Butler's seminar "Os fins da democracia" on 7 to 9 November 2017. An anonymous online petition asking Sesc to cancel her visit reached 88,821 signatures, and about 386 negative reviews appeared on the Sesc Pompeia Facebook page in about 24 hours from 26 October. About 3,000 people posted positive reviews in a counter-campaign (Vermelho, 1 November 2017, a partisan outlet that frames the episode as censorship).
The actors were the petitioners and the reviewers. Vermelho does not report that Sesc cancelled the seminar or censored anything; Sesc representatives declined to comment.
In December 2018, before taking office, Paulo Guedes called for cuts of up to 50% in Sistema S funding; the Confederação Nacional da Indústria rejected the idea (Congresso em Foco).

A 2019 bill by deputy Eli Borges, PL 6505/19, would make contributions to the Sistema S, including Sesc, optional and cap them at 1% of payroll, arguing that they burden employers (Jornal Contábil, 3 May 2021).
Provisional Measure 932/2020 cut contributions to the Sistema S entities, Sesc among them, by 50% until 30 June 2020 to relieve payrolls during the pandemic (Congresso em Foco, 1 April 2020).
Sesc São Paulo is funded through this levy, so the proposals concern its main income. The Butler petition targeted Sesc Pompeia's programme, not the levy.
details.bottom_line: The money is a levy on Brazilian companies in commerce, services and tourism, with no corporate sponsor reported. The weak points are that no São Paulo revenue figures were found, and that the levy has been the target of political proposals to cut or make it optional. Worth watching: published accounts, and any change to the levy.

name: Dazibao
funding: An exhibition page lists support from the Conseil des arts et des lettres du Québec, Canada Council, Conseil des arts de Montréal, Ville de Montréal and the Quebec culture ministry.

overview: Contemporary art centre and non-profit organisation at 5455 de Gaspé Avenue, suite 109 (ground floor), Montréal, in the Mile End (stated by the space; e-flux directory).

Founded in 1980 as one of the first Quebec and Canadian centres devoted exclusively to photography. It has embraced the full range of image-based practices since the early 1990s, moved to Pôle de Gaspé in 2014 and developed a digital component in 2020 (stated by the space).

Mandate: "an exhibition center dedicated to the dissemination and outreach of contemporary image-based practices", presenting local and international work and supporting artists over long periods (stated by the space).
Programme: exhibitions, residencies, sessions, publications (Les Portables, Monographies, Les Essais, Les Études), a bookshop, a video library and outreach projects.

Visiting: gallery open Tuesday to Saturday, 12 pm to 5 pm. Offices Tuesday to Friday, 10 am to 5 pm. Entry is free. A wheelchair-accessible ramp is on the building's northwest side and the gallery is on the ground floor.
details.funding_verdict: Dazibao: public support: Quebec, Canadian and Montreal arts councils and governments
funding: Dazibao states that it receives financial support from the Conseil des arts et des lettres du Québec, the Canada Council for the Arts, the Conseil des arts de Montréal, the ministère de la Culture et des Communications and the Ville de Montréal (Dazibao call for proposals page).
details.bottom_line: Dazibao is a not-for-profit centre that receives financial support from the Conseil des arts et des lettres du Québec, the Canada Council for the Arts, the Conseil des arts de Montréal, the Quebec culture ministry and the City of Montreal. Entry is free.

name: CRAC Valparaíso (Centro de Residencias de Arte Contemporáneo)
funding: It describes itself as self-sustained since 2007.

overview: Collaborative non-profit platform for socio-artistic productions across the city of Valparaíso, with offices at Avenida Prat 798, oficina 574 (TransArtists).
Self-sustained since 2007, as a project with a flexible, autonomous management model (TransArtists; Dutch Art Institute).

Residencies for artists and researchers are treated as city practices. Residents often run temporary community actions such as talks, workshops, performances and seminars. Residencies last one to three months, and applications are accepted on an ongoing basis (TransArtists).

It also runs a public community archive, a printed publication and a digital publisher. Listed focus areas are research residencies, water and coastal work, urban projects and socially engaged practice (TransArtists).

Accommodation is a room in the historic district or a similar space. The offices have work tables, wireless internet and a documentary archive on contemporary art, the public sphere, and city and territory (TransArtists).
details.funding_verdict: CRAC Valparaíso: self-sustained non-profit, as stated by CRAC
funding: TransArtists and the Dutch Art Institute both state that CRAC has been "self-sustained since 2007".
details.bottom_line: CRAC Valparaíso is described by TransArtists and the Dutch Art Institute as a self-sustained, independent non-profit platform for residencies in Valparaíso, running since 2007. That is the platform's own description.

name: Guangdong Museum
funding: In 2003 the Guangdong provincial authorities committed 884.2 million yuan (about $129.39 million) to build the new facility (China Daily). The page read did not state operating funding.
watch: The provincial museum of Guangdong; the older museum opened in 1959 and a new 67,000 square metre building was funded by the provincial government.
records_note: The page read showed no published accounts.

overview: The provincial museum of Guangdong in the Cultural and Art Square, Zhujiang New Town, Tianhe District (China Daily).
The older museum and the Guangzhou Lu Xun Memorial Hall opened to the public on 1 October 1959; the new building covers 67,000 square metres (China Daily).
What is there: four sections covering history, nature, art and temporary exhibitions on Guangdong and Lingnan culture (China Daily). The page read gave no collection size.
Archive: the page read did not mention an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Guangdong Museum: provincial government build, operating funding not stated
details.bottom_line: Construction was paid by the provincial government. Operating funding and any loans controversy were not found in the page read.

name: Nanjing Museum
funding: The pages read did not state who funds the museum. The Jiangsu provincial government and its culture bodies supervise it, per the 2026 probe reporting.
watch: In February 2026 a probe into the 1959 donation of 137 paintings by the Pang family found works sold off in the 1990s; the museum apologised, 29 people were implicated and the National Cultural Heritage Administration ordered a nationwide museum audit.
records_note: The pages read did not show published accounts.

overview: A provincial museum in Nanjing, Jiangsu (Sixth Tone, 10 February 2026).
The pages read did not state the opening year.
What is there: the Pang family donated 137 paintings in 1959; 132 remain in the collection (China Daily, 10 February 2026). The probe compared 30,255 calligraphy and painting artifacts (China Daily).
Archive: the pages read did not mention an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Nanjing Museum: provincial institution, funding not stated in the pages read
funding: The pages read did not itemise funding. Provincial bodies, the Jiangsu Provincial Department of Culture and Tourism and the Cultural Heritage Bureau, are named as supervisors (China Daily, 10 February 2026).

red_flags.heading: Looted or contested holdings
points: Jiangnan Spring, a Ming work estimated at 88 million yuan ($12.5 million), appeared at a Beijing auction in 2025 and was withdrawn in May 2025 after the donor's descendant reported it; it was donated with 136 other paintings in 1959 (China Daily, 10 February 2026).

The probe, guided by the National Cultural Heritage Administration, covered 12 provinces, 65,000 documents and over 1,100 interviews. It found that in the 1990s then executive vice director Xu Huping approved transfers of donated works to a state-owned dealership for sale, and that in July 1997 a custodian surnamed Zhang cut the listed price of Jiangnan Spring from 25,000 yuan to 2,500 yuan, bought it through an intermediary and resold it for 120,000 yuan (Sixth Tone, 10 February 2026).

Twenty-nine people were implicated, five of them dead; Xu is under investigation and the province directed administrative cases against the museum. Three paintings were recovered and one was found in a museum warehouse; Pine Breeze and Temple is still missing (China Daily, 10 February 2026).
The museum apologised and pledged new donation rules, stronger internal controls and public supervision. No verdicts had been reported (Sixth Tone, 10 February 2026).

details.bottom_line: The money story is about donated works sold off cheaply and resold. Who funds the museum was not stated in the pages read. Watch for verdicts and for the nationwide audit.

name: National Centre for the Performing Arts (NCPA)
funding: The page read did not state funding.
watch: Beijing's national performing arts complex, designed by the French architect Paul Andreu, opened at the end of 2007 with its own chorus, orchestra and opera singers.
records_note: The page read showed no published accounts.

overview: A theatre complex of 21.75 hectares beside a lake at 2 West Chang'an Avenue, Beijing (China Daily).
Opened at the end of 2007; designed by Paul Andreu (China Daily).
What is there: an opera theatre with a multifunction stage and elevating orchestra pit, and resident chorus, orchestra and opera singers (China Daily).
Archive: the page read did not mention an archive.
details.funding_verdict: National Centre for the Performing Arts: funding not stated in the page read
funding: The page read gave no construction cost, subsidy or sponsor.
details.bottom_line: The page read says nothing of money. A state filing or the centre's own accounts would be needed.
